keyPoints: Ovary structure: cortex with follicles and medulla with connective tissue
Ovary functions: oogenesis and hormone secretion (estrogen and progesterone)
Oviduct regions: infundibulum, ampulla, isthmus, and intramural part
Oviduct wall layers: serous membrane, muscular layer, and mucous membrane with cilia
Oviduct functions: ovum transport, sperm transport, fertilization site, and embryo nourishment

modelAnswer:
The ovary is a female reproductive gland located on either side of the uterus. It has a dual structure: the outer cortex contains follicles at various stages of development, while the inner medulla contains connective tissue, blood vessels, and nerves. The ovary performs two main functions: (1) Oogenesis - production of ova (egg cells) through meiosis, and (2) Endocrine function - secretion of hormones estrogen and progesterone that regulate the menstrual cycle and maintain pregnancy.

The oviduct (fallopian tube) is a muscular tube extending from the ovary to the uterus. Structurally, it consists of four regions: the infundibulum (funnel-shaped opening with fimbriae), ampulla (widest section), isthmus (narrow middle portion), and intramural part (embedded in uterine wall). The oviduct wall has three layers: outer serous membrane, middle muscular layer (circular and longitudinal smooth muscle), and inner mucous membrane with ciliated epithelium.

Functions of the oviduct include: (1) Ovum transport - ciliated cells and muscular contractions move the ovum toward the uterus, (2) Sperm transport - provides passage for sperm moving toward the ovum, (3) Fertilization site - the ampulla is where sperm typically fertilizes the ovum, and (4) Early embryo nourishment - the oviduct secretes nutrients supporting early embryonic development during its 3-4 day journey to the uterus.

topicTitle: 11.2 Female Reproductive Cycle and Hormonal Regulation
explanation: The uterine lining (endometrium) starts breaking down due to decreased concentration of progesterone. When progesterone levels drop sharply after the corpus luteum degenerates (if fertilization does not occur), the endometrium loses its hormonal support, leading to menstruation. Estrogen levels also decline but progesterone withdrawal is the primary trigger for endometrial breakdown.
